cards.back: The doctrine of the 'last things' (Greek eschata): death, Christ's return, resurrection, judgment, the millennium and the new creation.
Greek for 'presence' or 'arrival'; the usual New Testament term for Christ's coming (e.g. Matthew 24:3; 1 Thessalonians 4:15).
The 'thousand years' of Revelation 20:1-6, during which Satan is bound and the saints reign with Christ. Its timing and nature divide the millennial views.
From Greek chilioi, 'thousand': the early church term for belief in a future earthly reign of Christ, held by Papias, Justin Martyr and Irenaeus.
Postmillennialism, amillennialism, historic premillennialism and dispensational premillennialism (the line-up of Clouse's The Meaning of the Millennium, 1977).
Preterist (fulfilled in the first century), historicist (church history in sequence), futurist (mostly still future), idealist (timeless spiritual conflict). Many combine them (eclectic).
Inaugurated eschatology: the kingdom came with Christ's first coming but awaits consummation at his return. Associated with Vos, Cullmann and Ladd.
Jesus' teaching on the Mount of Olives about the temple's destruction and his coming: Matthew 24-25, Mark 13, Luke 21.
Daniel 9:24-27: seventy 'sevens' decreed for Daniel's people. Disputed whether the seventieth week follows directly or is separated by a gap.
The figure of 2 Thessalonians 2:3-12, variously identified as a future Antichrist, the papacy (historicism), or a first-century figure (preterism).
From Latin rapiemur in 1 Thessalonians 4:17: believers 'caught up' to meet the Lord. Views differ on timing: pre-, mid-, prewrath, post-tribulation.
Disputed: most scholars favour c. AD 95 under Domitian (Irenaeus); an early date of c. AD 65-68 is argued by Gentry and J. A. T. Robinson.
Christ's return in glory to judge the living and the dead, and the resurrection of the body. The creeds take no position on the millennium.
Christ returns after a long era of gospel triumph in which most of the world is converted through the Spirit's work.
Psalm 2; Psalm 110:1; Isaiah 2:2-4; Daniel 2:35, 44; Matthew 13:31-33; Matthew 28:18-20; 1 Corinthians 15:24-26; Romans 11:25-26.
Author of The Millennium (1957); defended postmillennialism in Clouse's Four Views (1977).
Author of He Shall Have Dominion (1992); a leading postmillennialist and partial preterist.
Anglican (1638-1726); his Treatise of the True Millennium (1703) systematised postmillennialism, though earlier Puritans held similar hopes.
Iain Murray's 1971 book tracing Puritan expectation of worldwide revival and the conversion of the Jews.
On 'Thy kingdom come': prays for the gospel's spread, the calling of the Jews and the fullness of the Gentiles. Postmillennialists cite it as expressing their hope.
The Congregationalist revision of Westminster, which adds an expectation of a more peaceful and glorious condition for the churches in the latter days (26.5).
American theologian (1703-1758) whose History of the Work of Redemption expressed postmillennial hope linked to revival.
Charles Hodge, A. A. Hodge and B. B. Warfield, nineteenth-century Reformed theologians who expected the gospel's worldwide triumph.
Revivalist (Murray, Mathison) and theonomic/Reconstructionist (Rushdoony, Bahnsen, Gentry).
Often attributed to the world wars and association with the liberal social gospel. Revived from the 1970s.
The thousand years of Revelation 20 symbolise the present age, in which Christ reigns and Satan is bound, ending with one return, resurrection and judgment.
Jay E. Adams's suggested name for amillennialism (1959 book later reissued as The Time Is at Hand), stressing that the millennium is now.
Christ's first coming restrained Satan from deceiving the nations (Matthew 12:29; Revelation 20:3), so the gospel goes worldwide.
A spiritual reality: regeneration, or the believer's soul entering Christ's presence at death to reign with him (Revelation 20:4).
Read the thousand years as the church age; became the dominant view in the Western church for centuries.
Fourth-century Donatist exegete whose symbolic reading of Revelation influenced Augustine.
Author of The Bible and the Future (1979); defended amillennialism in Clouse's Four Views.
Author of A Case for Amillennialism (2003; expanded 2013), stressing the two-age structure.
This age and the age to come, divided by Christ's return (Luke 20:34-36), leaving no room for a further earthly millennium.
Revelation repeats the history between the comings in seven parallel sections (Hendriksen's More Than Conquerors).
John 5:28-29: an 'hour' in which all the dead rise, some to life and some to judgment.
Rejects the 'Jewish opinions' of an earthly kingdom of the godly before the resurrection of the dead.
Christ returns once, after the tribulation, raises believers and reigns on earth for a millennium before the final judgment.
Fuller Seminary scholar; The Blessed Hope (1956) and The Gospel of the Kingdom; leading modern historic premillennialist.
Papias, Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 80-81) and Irenaeus (Against Heresies Book 5).
In Revelation 20:4-5 'came to life' should mean bodily resurrection both times, so two bodily resurrections frame the millennium (Henry Alford).
Christ the firstfruits, then those who are his at his coming, then the end: an interval may fall between the coming and the end.
The church endures the tribulation and meets Christ in the air as he comes to earth. Defended by Gundry (1973) and Moo (1984).
One people of God, with many expecting a future turning of ethnic Israel to Christ (Romans 11:25-26).
Edited by Craig Blomberg and Sung Wook Chung; essays defending the view against dispensational and amillennial alternatives.
Rapture in the second half of Daniel's seventieth week, before God's wrath. Associated with Marvin Rosenthal and Alan Kurschner.
Pictures death still occurring but at great age in the new order. Premillennialists see an interim kingdom; amillennialists read it as poetic imagery.
Systematic theologian who defends historic premillennialism in his Systematic Theology.
A pretribulational rapture, a seven-year tribulation, Christ's return, and a literal millennium fulfilling God's promises to national Israel.
Plymouth Brethren leader (1800-1882) who systematised dispensationalism and the pretribulational rapture.
Prophecy meetings (1831-1833) hosted by Lady Theodosia Powerscourt in County Wicklow, Ireland, where Darby's views developed.
C. I. Scofield's study Bible, published by Oxford University Press, which spread dispensationalism widely.
Read as a future seven-year tribulation, separated from the first sixty-nine weeks by the church age (Daniel 9:27).
Christ may come for his church at any moment with no prophesied event first, supporting a pretribulational rapture.
Christ comes for his saints (rapture) and later with his saints (Revelation 19:11-21) to set up the millennial kingdom.
Author of Things to Come (1958), a comprehensive dispensational eschatology.
Dallas Seminary president; The Rapture Question (1957), The Millennial Kingdom and The Revelation of Jesus Christ (1966).
Co-founded the Pre-Trib Research Center with Tim LaHaye; defends pretribulationism.
1 Thessalonians 1:10; 5:9; Revelation 3:10: believers are not appointed to wrath.
Blaising, Bock and Saucy (1993): Christ already reigns on David's throne in an inaugurated sense, with a future for national Israel.
Many prophecies, including much of the Olivet Discourse and Revelation, were fulfilled in AD 66-70; the bodily return, resurrection and judgment remain future.
From Latin praeteritus, 'gone by': prophecy viewed as fulfilled in the past.
'This generation' is read as Jesus' contemporaries, who saw the temple destroyed in AD 70.
Spanish Jesuit whose Vestigatio arcani sensus in Apocalypsi (1614) is often called the first systematic preterist commentary.
The Last Days According to Jesus (1998): argued for a largely preterist reading of the Olivet Discourse.
Gentry's case for dating Revelation c. AD 65-66, before the temple's destruction. The date is disputed.
Nero Caesar in Hebrew letters (Nrwn Qsr) totals 666; the variant 616 fits a Latin spelling.
Old Testament language for God's judgment (Isaiah 19:1), read as Christ's judgment on Jerusalem in Matthew 24:30.
Jewish historian whose Jewish War records the siege and fall of Jerusalem in AD 70.
Author of Last Days Madness; a leading popular partial preterist and postmillennialist.
The Days of Vengeance (1987), a preterist and postmillennial commentary on Revelation.
Partial affirms a future bodily Second Coming and resurrection (Acts 1:11; 1 Corinthians 15); full places them in the first century.
All biblical prophecy, including the Second Coming, resurrection and judgment, was fulfilled by AD 70.
Consistent preterism, covenant eschatology; critics often say hyper-preterism.
The Spirit of Prophecy (1971) and The Cross and the Parousia of Christ (1987); proposed a corporate covenantal resurrection.
The Parousia (1878): argued all New Testament references to Christ's coming point to AD 70.
Contemporary full preterist author and debater.
Resurrection as the people of God passing from the old covenant to the new, completed in AD 70.
Critics note the creeds confess a future return and bodily resurrection; full preterists answer that Scripture outranks the creeds.
Keith Mathison's edited Reformed critique of full preterism.
Hymenaeus and Philetus said the resurrection had already happened; critics see a parallel.
Christ will come 'in the same way' he ascended; critics read this as a visible bodily return.
If the Olivet coming was in AD 70, full preterists argue all coming and resurrection texts belong there too.
Revelation forecasts church and world history in sequence from the apostles to Christ's return.
A prophetic day equals a year (Numbers 14:34; Ezekiel 4:6), so 1,260 days means 1,260 years.
The papacy as an office; held by Luther, Calvin and the original Westminster Confession (25.6).
Clavis Apocalyptica (1627); Cambridge scholar who revived premillennialism among English Puritans.
Observations upon the Prophecies of Daniel and the Apocalypse of St. John (1733).
Horae Apocalypticae (1844), four volumes of historicist commentary.
American Presbyterian whose Notes on the New Testament follow a historicist reading of Revelation.
Many historicists saw the fifth and sixth trumpets (Revelation 9) as the Saracen and Turkish invasions.
The major modern tradition that retains historicism.
Interpreters disagree widely and often place the climax in their own day; date-setting (e.g. 1844) failed.
The leading Protestant approach from the Reformation until the mid-nineteenth century.
Most of Revelation (usually chapters 4-22) describes events still future, clustered around Christ's return.
Spanish Jesuit (1537-1591) whose Revelation commentary (c. 1590) put most of the book in a future three and a half years under one Antichrist.
Jesuit cardinal who also argued for a future individual Antichrist against the Protestant view.
Chilean Jesuit; The Coming of Messiah in Glory and Majesty, under the name Juan Josafat Ben-Ezra; Edward Irving's English translation, 1827.
Irenaeus and Hippolytus expected a future personal Antichrist and tribulation.
'Come up here': some dispensationalists see a picture of the rapture before the judgments.
The Revelation of Jesus Christ (1966), a classic dispensational futurist commentary.
Ladd's view: the end-time events are future, but without a pretribulational rapture or Israel-church division.
Some dispensationalists read Revelation 2-3 as foreshadowing successive stages of church history.
The cosmic judgments, bodily resurrection and new creation plainly have not yet happened.
Time texts such as Revelation 1:1, 3 and 22:10 suggest nearness for first readers; futurists answer with imminence and certainty.
Revelation depicts in symbols the conflict between God and evil throughout the church age, ending in Christ's victory.
The spiritual, symbolic or poetic approach.
Fourth-century Donatist whose symbolic reading influenced Augustine.
More Than Conquerors (1939): seven parallel sections, each spanning the first to the second coming.
Scottish scholar (1880s) who read Revelation as principles rather than predictions of specific events.
NIGTC Revelation (1999): a 'redemptive-historical' modified idealism with a future consummation.
Recapitulation: Revelation's cycles cover the same period from different angles, with growing intensity.
Every generation of Christians can read the book as addressed to its own struggles.
May detach the book from concrete history; idealists reply that the symbols name real patterns and a real end.
Triumph of the Lamb (2001), a Reformed, broadly idealist commentary on Revelation.
Revelation addressed its first readers, applies to every age, and points to a future end, so several approaches are combined.
Revelation: Four Views (1997; rev. 2013), a parallel commentary of historicist, preterist, futurist and spiritual views.
Eclectic or 'redemptive-historical' modified idealism, combining idealist, preterist and futurist elements.
NIV Application Commentary on Revelation (2000), rooted in the first-century Roman setting.
BECNT Revelation (2002), an eclectic and premillennial reading.
The Theology of the Book of Revelation and The Climax of Prophecy (1993), stressing Old Testament allusion and critique of Rome.
Things seen, things that are, things to come: read by some as signalling the book's mixed timeframe.
Respects historical setting, present relevance and future hope at once.
Can seem arbitrary; eclectics reply that genre, context and allusion guide each choice.
Not tied to one view: amillennial (Beale), premillennial (Osborne), and some postmillennial.
Scripture is organised around God's covenants, with one people of God and one covenant of grace across both testaments.
The eternal agreement between the Father and the Son to save the elect.
God's covenant with Adam before the fall, promising life for obedience (Genesis 2:16-17; Romans 5:12-21).
God's single gracious covenant through Christ, administered differently in the Old and New Testaments.
The classic confessional statement of the covenants of works and grace.
Dutch theologian; The Economy of the Covenants (1677).
Seventeenth-century Dutch theologian who developed federal theology.
One people of God; Galatians 3:29; Ephesians 2:11-22; Romans 11's single olive tree.
Reformed Baptist covenant theology: the new covenant is made only with the regenerate, hence believer's baptism.
Princeton biblical theologian; The Pauline Eschatology (1930) and the two-age framework.
Mostly amillennial or postmillennial, with some historic premillennialists.
Read as fulfilled and expanded in the new creation (Romans 4:13; Hebrews 11:16).
A framework that distinguishes stages of God's administration in history and holds that Israel and the church are distinct, with Israel's promises still to be fulfilled.
Greek for 'stewardship' or 'administration' (Ephesians 1:10; 3:2); the source of the term dispensation.
Innocence, conscience, human government, promise, law, grace, kingdom.
Israel-church distinction, consistently literal (normal) interpretation, and the glory of God as history's purpose (Dispensationalism Today, 1965).
Darby, Scofield, Chafer: heavenly and earthly peoples with separate destinies.
Ryrie, Walvoord, Pentecost: moderated the heavenly-earthly dualism while keeping the Israel-church distinction.
Blaising, Bock, Saucy (1990s): one unfolding kingdom with an inaugurated Davidic reign.
The church age was unrevealed in Old Testament prophecy (Ephesians 3:3-6).
Founded 1924 by Lewis Sperry Chafer; the leading dispensational school.
Late nineteenth-century meetings that spread premillennialism in North America.
Has the Church Replaced Israel? (2010); defends a future for national Israel.
The New Testament reads Israel's promises as fulfilled in Christ; dispensationalists reply that it reaffirms them (Romans 11:26-29).
God's plan unfolds through successive biblical covenants that find their fulfilment in Christ and the new covenant.
Peter Gentry and Stephen Wellum (2012; 2nd ed. 2018): the defining work.
Refers to the progressive revelation of God's plan across the covenants.
Creation (Adam), Noah, Abraham, Israel (Moses), David, and the new covenant.
A middle way between covenant theology and dispensationalism.
Believer's baptism, since the new covenant community is regenerate (Jeremiah 31:31-34).
Typologically expanded to the whole new creation (Romans 4:13).
Types escalate through the covenants toward Christ.
A related movement (Tom Wells, Fred Zaspel) stressing the newness of the new covenant.
Edited by Stephen Wellum and Brent Parker; essays developing the framework.
Usually amillennial, sometimes historic premillennial.

cards.front: The Spiritual Understanding in one sentence
cards.back: Revelation is the unveiling of Jesus Christ and his finished work, read as present spiritual reality rather than a forecast to fear.
The Lamb standing as though slain (Revelation 5:6): the Lion conquers by self-giving, and the cross is the centre of history.
John 19:30; Revelation 16:17; Revelation 21:6. The judgments unfold a victory already won at the cross.
Babylon (religion of mixture and self-effort, the commerce of the soul) versus the New Jerusalem (the Bride, grace coming down from above).

cards.front: Mark of the beast vs seal of God
cards.back: A mind and life shaped by flesh, fear and self-effort versus the Spirit and the Father's name on the forehead: a new identity (Revelation 13:16; Revelation 14:1).
Humanity's number: human effort that falls short of God's sabbath rest (7).
12 × 12 × 1,000: the complete people of God, seen again as the innumerable multitude (Revelation 7:4-9).

cards.front: The thousand years and first resurrection
cards.back: The fullness of Christ's present reign; the first resurrection is the new birth into union with him (Revelation 20:4-6; Ephesians 2:6).
Life by union with Christ (the tree of life, Revelation 22:2) set against living by the knowledge of good and evil.
Idealism and partial preterism (symbolic, rooted in the first century), and amillennial or postmillennial 'present reign' views; it differs most from futurism.
